## Christina Higgins*
## Toward un-WEIRDing academic publishing about language [Applied Linguistics]
[https://doi.org/10.1515/ijsl-2024-0073](https://doi.org/10.1515/ijsl-2024-0073) Received May 13, 2024; accepted August 20, 2024
Abstract: In this commentary, I reflect on the shortcomings in representing linguistic knowledge in academic publishing. While Klein's 1989 article Schreiben oder Lesen, aber nicht beides, oder: Vorschlag zur Wiedereinführung der Keilschrift mittels Hammer und Meißel calls attention to the overproduction of scholarly knowledge in the context of publish or perish ideologies, I invite us to consider how we distribute knowledge within the spaces of academic publishing with regard to global north and global south scholars and contexts. At present, scholarship about language is largely produced by scholars in WEIRD contexts, that is, western, educated, industrial, rich, democratic societies. This leads to limited outcomes in terms of what we can find out about the nature of language by virtue of excluding a majority of the world's populations and contexts. As we go about questioning the purpose of academic publishing, we also need to consider how to better represent our findings in light of the narrowness of what we have researched.
Keywords: academic publishing; global north; global south; knowledge production; representation
Klein'[s (1989)](#page-4-0) essay calls attention to the overproduction of scholarly knowledge in the context of publish or perish ideologies. I echo his concern and attempt to draw attention to the question of whose knowledge production we are engaged in as readers, scholars, and editors.
Since the time of his writing, the number of journals that focus on language and linguistics has multiplied, thus making Klein's observation even more important to address. Attention to citation metrics and h-indexes has exacerbated the problem and has created anxiety among many scholars who are simply following the apparent "rules of the game" by publishing non-stop. While this is a problem that needs many solutions, a major part of the problem is that we hear the same voices over and over again because of the imperative to publish so often. While serving as an editor for Applied Linguistics for five years, I received frequent submissions by the
^(*)Corresponding author: Christina Higgins, Second Language Studies, University of Hawaii at Manoa, 1890 East West Rd, Honolulu, Hawaii, 96826, USA, E-mail:[ cmhiggin@hawaii.edu](mailto:cmhiggin@hawaii.edu)
same young, aspiring scholars affiliated with resource-rich universities, largely in the global north, who were eager to have their work published in our journal, with some individuals submitting three to four new manuscripts a year. Since the goal of any journal is to represent a diverse set of research in the field, I reached out to several of these serial submitters directly to encourage them to broaden their readership by publishing in a wider range of journals. In at least one case, the author had already done this, and explained that he was eager to publish numerous papers (with slightly different angles) at the same time in all of the top journals. While the papers this scholar submitted were of high quality, it became necessary to set an internal policy of only considering one paper at a time by any lead author, in order to attract a wider array of authors and topics.
While this policy change became necessary, our editorial team was also tackling the problem of seldom receiving high quality submissions by scholars from underrepresented contexts working on languages other than English. I began to try to address this issue by actively reaching out to presenters at conferences that I attended to encourage them to submit, and by engaging in email conversations with scholars whose work I felt would be of interest to our journal. This required extra effort of course, as many of these scholars were not in our editorial team's usual academic circles of engagement. Even with these efforts, we saw little change in terms of what kinds of scholars and contexts our journal represented. Submissions which were lacking in methodological rigor or up-to-date literature reviews had little chance of making it through external review because of a lack of resources. It is a difficult problem to solve since there is a deep imbalance for scholars in the global south in terms of access to cutting-edge research methods and approaches, library holdings, and support for academic publishing. The result is that our journal has rarely published papers about language practices in the global south, or which embraced ways of thinking about language which might also have local relevance beyond global north contexts.
There are efforts at some journals to develop submission procedures wherein a member of the editorial team agrees to work with a submitting author to ensure that their paper has a better chance of making it through initial rounds of review. These editors become co-authors of these papers to receive credit for their work. If more journals were able to offer this co-authorship, more knowledge from underrepresented contexts would better circulate in our academic publishing spaces.
Publishing a wider array of authors will lead to new forms of scholarly knowledge, thus enriching disciplinary understandings. More than a decade ago, scholars in psychology began to draw attention to the problem of the representation in knowledge production, as demonstrated through published academic research. The problem is that most psychology studies are led by WEIRD scholars and are carried out in WEIRD contexts, that is, research western, educated, industrial, rich,
democratic societies ([Arnett 2008;](#page-4-1)[ Henrich et al. 2010)](#page-4-2). The reason for this is that most well-resourced universities are located in the global north, and most grantfunded research is distributed in these institutions as well. In psychology and other fields, the problem that ensues is that the research produced in these WEIRD locations is presented as applying universally to all populations, which is not empirically valid. Another problem is that WEIRD science thus dictates trends in research based on research conducted on a small portion of the world's population. [Arnett (2008)](#page-4-1) shows that psychological research published in APA journals, for instance, over-represents Americans, who are less than 5 % of the world's population yet who are the participants in most of the research.
In research on language, the picture is quite similar. For example, research which used the term "family language policy" (FLP) from 2008 to 2020 revealed that while the field has increasingly diversified, the language most investigated is English, and the most studied context for participants is the United States [(Lanza](#page-4-3) [and Gomes 2020](#page-4-3)). To move beyond this state of affairs, I worked with Lyn Wright to try to broaden the scope of FLP research, and we published an edited volume titled Diversifying Family Language Policy [(Wright and Higgins 2022)](#page-4-4), which intended to better represent all aspects of this field by including scholars from the global south, research on under-represented populations and contexts, and a wider understanding of the concept of family itself. While we feel that we were partially successful in achieving diversification away from WEIRD scholarship, we failed in some aspects. First, it was difficult to identify scholars who are located in the global south who have the resources they need to conduct research and engage in academic publishing. Of the 15 chapters, only two are co-authored by scholars from highly underrepresented nations – Iran and Chile – and these authors were located at global north universities. One chapter was authored by two scholars in South Africa about FLP in Cape Town. All of the other chapters reported on studies that were possible because lead authors or senior scholars were involved in the process, and they were all located at research-intensive, global north universities in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Finland, Sweden, and Australia. The diversity we were more successful at representing in the end was a wider array of family types that have previously been ignored in FLP research, including families with single parents, families with LGBTQ parents, multilingual Deaf-Hearing families, and families that ascribed to detraditionalized notions of familyhood. Geographically and linguistically, the volume expanded horizons by including studies on languages that are under-reported in the literature, including Somali, British Sign Language, Turkmen, Persian, Arabic, Hawaiian, Setswana, isiXhosa, and Chedungun. Still, there is much room for improvement in terms of representing what is known about how multilingual people manage their languages in family life.
The field of FLP is more diverse than other language sub-fields, and thus provides an illustration of language research that is at least on track to become less WEIRD. Most other sub-fields are just beginning to consider this as a problem. The field of SLA has been identified as particularly lacking in terms of non-WEIRD languages, participants, and contexts, as much of the research draws its conclusions from studies involving university students in the global north [(Andringa and](#page-4-5) [Godfroid 2020)](#page-4-5). There have been some explicit efforts to expand beyond non-WEIRD contexts, including a special issue of Language Learning ([Godfroid and](#page-4-6) [Andringa 2023](#page-4-6)) that invited contributions which could report on studies that involve replication from an influential study based on a WEIRD context in a non, or less-WEIRD context, among people with varying degrees of education. While all of the scholars were located in well-resourced, western universities, the six studies involved more diversity among participants than is typical in SLA research, including part-time English learners in the UK, school children in rural Côte d'Ivoire, non-college educated adults in the U.S., young adults in Sri Lanka who were taking English classes to improve their social status, high school students in Bosnia and Italy, and high school students in Flanders, Belgium. Only two of the six studies were able to demonstrate replication of results, thus raising important questions about the universality of the initial studies involving college-educated language learners in global north contexts and drawing attention to the methodological challenges of replication as well. This set of papers adds to previous work that questioned the generalizability of SLA findings for all, including[ Bigelow et al.](#page-4-7) [(2006),](#page-4-7) which found that language learners with limited schooling engaged in noticing and recalling feedback quite differently than more educated and literate learners. While the noticing hypothesis has long been treated as a critical element for successful SLA, such research has demonstrated that it is not always relevant in a range of contexts.
When scholars whose languages and contexts have heretofore been underrepresented are able to contribute to these discussions, it is likely that concepts and knowledge about language that we treat as gold standards will be challenged, and for the better. As an illustration, there has already been increased debate on the relevance of the native speaker as the baseline in the fields of Applied Linguistics [(Davies 2003)](#page-4-8) and SLA ([Ortega 2013)](#page-4-9), and this construct has been increasingly challenged due to its relationship with linguistic imperialism and global north hegemony in the field of English as an international language. The benefit of the multilingual turn in these fields is that there are now studies that examine multilingual acquisition without measuring language proficiency as the sum of multiple monolinguals. The term native speaker itself has little meaning in many parts of the world, where being multilingual is taken for granted and is itself a baseline for asking questions about language.
It would benefit all of us if we could provide more of our publishing spaces to researchers who are questioning existing foundations of knowledge in new ways, simply by virtue of their geographic, social, and linguistic contexts, so that we can better see what we are really talking about when we discuss language. Rather than being lip service to diversity and inclusion for its own sake, knowledge production from underrepresented parts of the world will broaden all of our horizons.
Christina Higgins is the past Editor-in-Chief of Applied Linguistics.
